To demoralize someone means to weaken their spirit, confidence, and will to keep going. It's not just making someone feel sad — it specifically attacks their inner drive, their belief that they can succeed, and their desire to keep trying.

When someone is demoralized, they often feel:

  • Like there's no point in continuing
  • Like they are not capable or not good enough
  • Like nothing they do will make a difference
  • Like giving up is the only sensible option

1. In everyday life (the most common use): To cause a person or group to lose courage, confidence, and motivation — usually through repeated failures, harsh treatment, humiliation, or by making them feel hopeless.

"The manager's constant public criticism demoralized the entire team. People started putting in less effort and thinking about quitting."

"Failing the exam three times in a row completely demoralized her. She began to wonder if she was even capable of passing."

2. In military or strategic contexts: To weaken the fighting spirit of an enemy — to destroy their belief that they can win, so they lose the will to resist or fight.

"The surprise attack was designed not just to cause physical damage, but to demoralize the enemy troops."

"Enemy propaganda was used to demoralize soldiers by making them question whether the war was worth fighting."

Both uses share the same idea: something attacks the will from the inside, not just the body from the outside.
The Key Difference: Sad vs. Demoralized

This is an important distinction.

You can be sad but still motivated. If your team loses a match, you might feel sad — but you still want to train harder and win next time.

Being demoralized goes deeper. It shakes your belief that winning is even possible. A demoralized player doesn't just feel sad about losing — they start thinking, "What's the use? We can't win anyway." The sadness is in the emotions; the demoralization is in the will.

This is why the word is stronger than simply "upset" or "sad."

There is a scale.

  • Slightly demoralized: A bit shaken. Less confident. Motivation has dipped, but the person is still functioning.
  • Severely demoralized: Completely crushed. The person (or group) has essentially given up mentally. They go through the motions but have no real belief or energy left.
What — or Who — Can Demoralize Someone?

Demoralization doesn't have to come from a person. It can come from:

  • A person — a harsh boss, a bully, an overly critical coach, a toxic colleague
  • A situation — an impossible workload, a system that keeps punishing you no matter what you do
  • Repeated experiences — failing again and again, being ignored, being unfairly treated
  • Circumstances — being vastly outnumbered, losing resources, watching people around you give up

"The impossible deadlines and lack of support slowly demoralized even the most dedicated workers."

"Three straight seasons of losses demoralized the fans and the players alike."

Yes, absolutely. You can demoralize yourself through your own thoughts and behaviors — by constantly focusing on your failures, telling yourself you're not good enough, or comparing yourself unfavorably to others.

"He demoralized himself by replaying every mistake he had ever made, until he convinced himself he wasn't capable of success."

There are words close in meaning to demoralize, but each one is slightly different:

  • Discourage — to make someone doubt whether they should bother trying. It's milder. You discourage someone from attempting something; you demoralize someone who is already trying.
  • Dishearten — to make someone feel sad and lose hope. More emotional, less about destroying the fighting will specifically.
  • Dispirit — very similar to dishearten; to drain someone's enthusiasm and energy.
  • Crush (informal) — a strong, vivid word, but it's often used loosely. Demoralize is more precise about what is being destroyed (the morale, the will, the belief in success).

Demoralize is the strongest and most specific of these. It particularly targets morale — the fighting spirit, the collective or individual belief in one's ability to succeed.
Grammar: How the Word Is Used

Demoralize is a transitive verb — it must act on someone. Something demoralizes someone or a group. It doesn't stand alone.

✅ "The defeat demoralized the soldiers."
✅ "The constant failures demoralized her."
✅ "They were completely demoralized." (passive form — very natural and common)
❌ "It demoralizes." ← incomplete; needs an object

Related forms of the word:

  • Demoralized (adjective): Describing a state. "He looked completely demoralized." "The demoralized team refused to play in the second half."
  • Demoralizing (adjective): Describing something that causes demoralization. "It was a demoralizing experience." "The working conditions were demoralizing."
  • Demoralization (noun): The process or state of being demoralized. "The demoralization of the workforce led to a sharp drop in productivity."

To demoralize someone is to destroy their inner motivation, confidence, and belief that things can get better or that they can succeed. It goes beyond making someone feel sad — it attacks the will itself. A demoralized person doesn't just feel bad; they feel like there's no point in trying anymore. It can happen through harsh people, impossible situations, repeated failures, or even one's own negative thinking. The effect can range from a slight loss of confidence to a complete collapse of fighting spirit.
